extracted.intended_audience: researchers, funders, research institutions, and stakeholders interested in open/preprint-first publishing and post-publication peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and operational standards for running a preprint-first publishing platform coupled to formal, invited post-publication peer review (the F1000Research/platforms model), covering checks, referee selection, report requirements, versioning, indexing thresholds, crediting reviewers, and infrastructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-publication checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Following article submission, an internal team (largely postdocs) conduct a series of pre-publication checks. These are significantly more rigorous than those typically conducted on traditional preprint servers and more closely resemble those found in journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checks include whether it is scientific work from a scientist; whether it is plagiarised; whether it meets ethical requirements; whether it is readable and meets community standards; whether source data are provided (which is required); and whether it adheres to FAIR principles. The team’s checks take a median of ~2 working days. On F1000Research ~75% of submissions passed checks; on Wellcome Open Research ~86% passed (rejections often due to lack of relevant grants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Source data availability and FAIR compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Source data must be provided and submissions should adhere to FAIR principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data availability is a required element of the pre-publication checks; compliance with FAIR increases accessibility and reusability. Platforms typeset articles with NLM-compliant XML and provide detailed metadata to maximise readability, accessibility, and text mining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication speed and production standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles that pass checks are published with a DOI and are typeset with NLM-compliant XML and associated detailed metadata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical timings reported: median ~2 working days for prepublication checks, production (including author proofing) median 4–5 working days, and total submission-to-publication median 14–16 working days (including author queries). Speed and metadata/licensing standards are part of the service quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author commitment to invited post-publication peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: At submission authors commit to immediate formal, post-publication, invited peer review; once published under this model, authors cannot send the article to a journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a contractual/procedural requirement differentiating the platform from a standalone preprint server and ensures the article enters the formal review workflow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee selection and conflict-of-interest checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors select referees from a provided list of acceptable referees or can suggest others; the internal team checks selected referees for relevant experience and obvious conflicts of interest before inviting approved referees on the authors’ behalf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite concerns about recruiting for open review, F1000 found recruitment feasible; for articles that 'passed' peer review the average number of reviewers invited is 10. The internal vetting for relevant experience and conflicts is an explicit quality control step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee status categories and required outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees are asked to give a status (approved; approved with reservations; not approved) and to provide a supporting referee report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports are produced via guided, structured forms that consider specific aspects depending on article type. The peer review questions focus on technical aspects, including the appropriateness of study designs and methods, and the extent to which the data support the conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured, technical focus of referee reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Referee guidance and forms prompt reviewers to focus on technical aspects such as study design, methods, and the extent of support for conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are structured forms tailored by article type. The platform is also developing separate tools to assess perceived impact and importance of findings. The emphasis is on technical rigor rather than purely subjective judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency: publishing and signing referee reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Referee reports are published alongside the article and are signed with the referees’ names and affiliations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing signed reports is intended to increase candour and constructiveness; F1000 observed referees taking the process more seriously and being more candid and constructive under transparent conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revisions, versioning, and author-driven responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors decide whether, how and when to respond to referees and whether they want to revise. New versions are published, added to the article history, and are independently citable; referees can update their approval status with each version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article title updates dynamically with version number and referee status. The ability to formally revise is essential and widely used by authors to address critical comments. There is no final unchangeable version—authors and referees can return at any time to make updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing criteria based on referee approvals
rubrics_metrics.description: Indexing in major bibliographic databases (e.g., PubMed, Scopus) is contingent on meeting peer review approval thresholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically, once an article achieves two 'Approved' statuses, or one 'Approved' and two 'Approved with Reservations', it is indexed; indexers then index all versions, past and future.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open community commenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Any researcher who provides their name and affiliation can comment throughout the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community comments are an ongoing option and complement invited referee reports; authors decide when to stop changing the article but comments remain possible at any time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refereeing process speed and hands-on editorial support
rubrics_metrics.description: The internal team manages logistics of the whole peer review process, which accelerates review turnaround; reviewers also receive credit for open peer review which encourages participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: F1000 attributes fast peer review to logistical management and credit mechanisms; hands-on editorial support aids authors and reviewers and contributes to high participation and speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit and recognition for referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review activity is made citable and discoverable to enable reviewer credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each referee report is assigned a DOI, can be included on ORCID profiles and in Publons. F1000 encourages invited referees to list co-referees to recognise early-career contributors; uptake of co-referee listing grew from 4% to 12% (2013–2017). ORCID indicates F1000 is a major source of referee reports on ORCID.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology and infrastructure integration
rubrics_metrics.description: The platform provides technical infrastructure to manage publishing, versioning, linking, and discovery, and integrates with core scholarly infrastructure providers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrations include bibliographic indexers, repositories and archives, ORCID, CrossRef, data & software repositories, visualization tools, impact & analysis tools, authoring tools, and reference management systems. Platform tools include referee finders, referee report authoring systems, and author tools to respond and update articles—important for handling the complexity introduced by versioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-driven governance and service-provider role
rubrics_metrics.description: The platform model is author-driven: there are no editors making acceptance decisions and researchers themselves are in charge of their article and make the key decisions; the platform views itself as a service provider to the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: F1000 frames its role as providing infrastructure, tools, and editorial services rather than controlling platforms; the approach prioritises researcher control and evolving platform features according to community needs.
